lead: A device that sends data to a cloud IoT platform gets four things without its owner building a server: a verified identity, a standard endpoint that speaks MQTT or AMQP over TLS, a stored copy of its last known state, and a rule engine that forwards each message to a database, a function or an alert. AWS IoT Core and Azure IoT Hub are the two most used examples. The same pattern — register, connect, publish, route, store — appears in every IoT product, from a farm's moisture sensors to a fleet of delivery bikes.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.1 for cloud models and elastic resources, and MQTT publish-subscribe from Unit 3.

sections.h3: Six services that replace your own servers

blocks.text: A farm with 500 soil-moisture devices needs four capabilities at once: proof that each device is genuine, an endpoint that can hold hundreds of open connections, a store for the readings, and a way to alert when a value crosses a limit. Built by hand this means an authentication server, a broker, a database and a script runner — each patched, scaled and paid for separately. A cloud IoT platform sells all of them as one managed service.

items: Device registry: one record per device holding its ID, credentials, model and enabled or disabled flag.
Secure endpoint: MQTT over TLS, AMQP 1.0 or HTTPS; the platform terminates TLS and authenticates the device.
Device shadow or twin: a JSON document holding the last reported and last desired state of the device.
Rules engine: filters messages by topic, payload or a query, and forwards the matches to other services.
Routing targets: object storage, NoSQL tables, message queues, serverless functions, alerting services.
Monitoring and device management: connection counts, error and throttling metrics, plus remote jobs and firmware updates.

blocks.text: Pricing follows usage: messages in and out, device-minutes connected, and operations such as shadow updates. Publishing every 10 seconds where the physics needs 10 minutes is the most common way to overspend.

The device registry is the authority. Registering a device creates a record with a unique device ID, its credentials and metadata such as model and location. Disabling the record stops connections at once, which is exactly what you want when a sensor is stolen.

AWS IoT Core issues an X.509 client certificate and key pair. The private key never leaves the device, and the device connects on port 8883 using mutual TLS — both sides present certificates. A policy attached to the certificate is a JSON document naming the topics the device may publish and subscribe to, so a hacked sensor can write to its own topic and nowhere else.

Azure IoT Hub uses a SAS token by default. A SAS (shared access signature) is a string carrying the hub's resource URI, an expiry time and a signature computed with the device's symmetric key. The device sends it in the connection string at each connect and simply builds a new one when it expires; X.509 is also supported. A SAS token is easy to compute on a small microcontroller, while a certificate needs a trusted clock and more memory.

A device shadow (AWS) or device twin (Azure) is a JSON document the platform stores for each device. Its desired section holds what the cloud wants, its reported section holds what the device last said, and the difference is the delta. A pump is offline during a Chennai power cut; you write desired state pump = off. On reconnect the device asks for the delta, sees the change and applies it. An app reads the same document to show last known state without waking the device.

A message arriving at the endpoint does nothing useful until it is routed. The rules engine matches on topic, payload or a query, then invokes actions in order. AWS uses a SQL-like statement, for example SELECT * FROM 'farm/+/moisture' WHERE moisture < 20. Azure uses message routing with a query string such as $body.moisture < 20. Both send matching messages to storage, queues and functions and drop the rest.
M_day = N × (1440 ÷ T)    and    B_day = M_day × b
blocks.where: M_day is messages per day; N is the number of devices; T is the publish interval in minutes; 1440 is the minutes in a day; B_day is bytes per day; b is bytes per message.

blocks.text: Monitoring closes the loop. Both platforms export metrics — connected devices, messages used against quota, throttled requests, errors by type — and these are the numbers worth alarming on.

examples.question: A farm runs 500 soil-moisture devices. Each device publishes one 200-byte message every 10 minutes. Find (a) messages per day for the whole farm, (b) data volume per day in MB using 1 MB = 10⁶ bytes, (c) the peak message rate in messages per second if all 500 devices publish inside one 60-second window, and (d) the average rate for comparison.
steps: Publishes per device per day = 1440 minutes ÷ 10 minutes = 144 messages.
Average rate = 72,000 ÷ 86,400 s = 0.83 messages/s, so the peak is about ten times the average — size buffers for the peak, not the average.
examples.answer: The farm sends 72,000 messages per day, 14.4 MB per day, with a peak burst of 8.33 messages/s against an average of 0.83 messages/s.
examples.check:
devices = 500
bytes_per_msg = 200
interval_min = 10
per_device_day = 1440 / interval_min
messages_day = devices * per_device_day
bytes_day = messages_day * bytes_per_msg
mb_day = bytes_day / 10**6
peak = devices / 60
average = messages_day / 86400
print(int(messages_day))
print(round(mb_day, 2))
print(round(peak, 2))
print(round(average, 2))

traps: AWS IoT Core and Azure IoT Hub are not just brokers. Exams ask separately for the device registry, the shadow or twin, and the rules engine.
Device shadow belongs to AWS, device twin to Azure. Swapping the names loses the mark even when the description is right.
MB here is 10⁶ bytes. If a question says MiB or 2²⁰, the answer changes: 14,400,000 bytes is 13.73 MiB, not 14.4 MiB.
Average rate and peak rate are different numbers. Use the publishing interval for daily volume and the burst window for peak.
A SAS token expires. A device with a wrong clock builds a token that looks already expired, and the hub refuses the connection.

quiz.q: Name four services an IoT cloud platform provides besides the message endpoint.
quiz.a: Device registry, device shadow or twin, rules engine or message routing, storage and function targets, and monitoring with device management.

quiz.q: Which port carries MQTT over TLS to AWS IoT Core, and what does the device present by default?
quiz.a: Port 8883, using mutual TLS with an X.509 client certificate and its private key.

quiz.q: Why does a device shadow let an application read a device's state without connecting to the device?
quiz.a: The platform stores the last reported state as a JSON document in the cloud. The application reads that document directly, so the device can be offline, asleep or behind a firewall and the last known values are still available.

quiz.q: Give two reasons to issue one credential per device instead of one shared password for the fleet.
quiz.a: Revoking or disabling one device leaves the rest working; a policy per credential limits each device to its own topics; and logs and usage bills point to a single device when something misbehaves.

quiz.q: 200 devices publish one 500-byte message every 5 minutes. Find messages per day, data per day in MB (1 MB = 10⁶ bytes), and the peak rate if all 200 publish within 60 s.
quiz.a: Per device per day = 1440 ÷ 5 = 288. Messages = 200 × 288 = 57,600 per day. Bytes = 57,600 × 500 = 28,800,000 bytes = 28.8 MB per day. Peak = 200 ÷ 60 = 3.33 messages/s.

quiz.q: A device's certificate expired at midnight. The platform refuses its connection, yet the rules engine shows no errors and the dashboard simply stops updating. Explain the failure point and where the fix belongs.
quiz.a: The TLS handshake fails before any MQTT packet is sent, so no message ever reaches a topic and the rules engine has nothing to reject. The dashboard sees stale data rather than an error. The fix belongs in device management and provisioning: renew the certificate, and automate renewal before expiry so no human has to visit the device.

beyond: Not for the exam. In production the rules often run at the edge: AWS IoT Greengrass and Azure IoT Edge place a local broker and rule engine on a gateway, so decisions survive a dropped link. Large fleets avoid loading credentials by hand — AWS fleet provisioning and the Azure Device Provisioning Service issue them on first boot. When message rates outgrow a rules engine, teams move to stream processors, the subject of Chapter 5.3. Search 'AWS IoT Core developer guide', 'Azure IoT Hub message routing' and 'device provisioning service' for current service names, which change every few years.
